match.reason: The closest card, The three-sector circular flow, explains the money loop but does not teach the knock-on chain from falling household spending to business sales, jobs, incomes and tax revenue, so it is related rather than the same idea.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, wording: The right option says the government 'has less to spend on services' as a certainty, while the card says lower tax 'can leave' it with less to spend. Governments can borrow or keep spending in a downturn, so the option should be hedged, for example 'may have less to spend'.

rejected.title: How the sectors depend on each other
card: Each sector in the circular flow relies on the others. Households need businesses for goods and jobs. Businesses need households to buy what they make.
Spending by one sector is income for another. Household spending is the sales of businesses.
So a change in one place spreads. If households cut their spending, business sales fall. Businesses may then cut jobs and hours, so household incomes fall.
Lower incomes and lower sales mean less tax paid to government. This can leave the government with less to spend on services.
rejected.remember: Spending is income for someone else, so a fall in one sector can spread to the others.

a.q: Households in Ballarat spend less in local shops. Which change is most likely to follow first?
opts: Shops make fewer sales
Shops make higher profits
Households earn more income
The government collects more tax
a.why: Household spending is the sales of businesses, so less spending means fewer sales. Profits and incomes are more likely to fall than rise, and tax revenue follows later.
a.clue: One sector's spending is another sector's income.

b.q: Many shoppers in Bendigo spend less, so a clothing shop cuts its staff hours. What is the likely effect on the government?
opts: Less tax is paid, so it has less to spend on services
More tax is paid, so it has more to spend on services
Tax paid is unchanged, so its spending stays the same
Less tax is paid, but only by the clothing shop owner
b.why: The shop's lower sales and the workers' fewer hours both mean lower incomes, so less tax is paid and the government is likely to have less to spend. The tempting option that only the shop owner pays less misses the workers, who also earn less and so pay less tax.
b.clue: Who earns less here: the shop, its workers, or both?

b.q: Many shoppers in a Bendigo town spend less, and a clothing shop cuts staff hours. What is the next likely effect on the government?
opts: It may collect less tax and have less to spend
It collects more tax, as shops need help
Its tax revenue stays the same in every case
It gains money, as households will save more
b.why: Lower sales and lower incomes mean less tax is paid, so the government may have less to spend. More tax would need more income, and the shop's cut in hours lowers income.
b.clue: Think about what workers and shops pay tax on.

b.best: It may collect less tax and have less to spend

problems.detail: The right option is the only one hedged with 'may'. The wrong options are absolute or come with odd reasons ('stays the same in every case', 'households will save more', 'shops need help'), so a student could pick the right one without knowing the idea.
'A Bendigo town' is confusing, because Bendigo is itself a city. 'Shoppers in Bendigo' would be clearer.

check.summary: The card and question a are correct. In question b the right option stands out as the only hedged one ('may') among absolute or implausible distractors, and 'a Bendigo town' is awkward wording.
